paper_metadata.title: Algorithms for quantum simulation at finite energies

summary: This paper introduces two gate-based quantum algorithms for finite-energy quantum simulation: a provably efficient cosine-filter method with runtime poly(N, 1/δ, 1/ε), and a quantum-assisted Monte Carlo scheme for microcanonical and canonical observables. The numerical demonstrations use an Ising benchmark with N=20 and N=100 spins, δ values of 0.1, 1, and 4, and about 10^5 Monte Carlo samples per point; no specific quantum hardware or practical quantum advantage is demonstrated.

experiments.description: Hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for computing expectation values of observables in a finite energy interval around an efficiently preparable initial state using a cosine filter and interferometric measurements.

hyperparameters.filter_width_delta: arbitrary; analyzed for constant and decreasing with N
hyperparameters.filter_parameter_x: used in expansions; examples x=3 and x=1
hyperparameters.r_parameter: optimized form uses r=0.4 or r=1 in examples
hyperparameters.energy_window: E in [E_psi - r sigma_psi, E_psi + r sigma_psi]

algorithm.parameter_initialization: Initial state psi is any efficiently preparable state; examples include product states and Fock-like states

problem_formulation.encoding_details: No qubit encoding of an optimization problem; the algorithm estimates observables after applying a cosine energy filter to an efficiently preparable state
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate A_{delta,psi}(E)=<psi|[A P_delta(E)+P_delta(E) A]|psi> / (2<psi|P_delta(E)|psi>) and related filtered observables
problem_formulation.problem_hamiltonian: H = sum_n h_n; local many-body Hamiltonian with spectrum in [-N/2, N/2]

problem_instance.description: Many-body spin Hamiltonian; numerical illustrations use an exactly solvable Ising model with N=100 spins and parameters g=1,h=2, plus other parameter settings in figures

dataset_specification.description: N=100 spins for main numerical examples; also N=20 in some Monte Carlo comparisons

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Numerical evaluation of filtered observables and comparison against exact calculations for selected states and observables

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Classical computation of cosine-filter coefficients and postprocessing of measured time-series data
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Classical summation of measured amplitudes with filter coefficients to reconstruct observables

results.value: E in [E_psi - r sigma_psi, E_psi + r sigma_psi]

classical_baselines.value: no classical algorithm achieving this polynomial scaling is known

speedup_claims.factor: polynomial scaling where no classical algorithm with the same scaling is known
speedup_claims.conditions: for efficiently preparable initial states and efficient measurement of aA,psi(t); time polynomial in N, 1/delta, and 1/epsilon
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper does not provide a concrete classical runtime for comparison; the claim is based on the absence of a known classical algorithm with the same scaling.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Polynomial-time access to interferometric measurements and state preparation; no concrete hardware resource estimate is given.
limiting_factors: Measurement count scales as O(sqrt(N)/delta * epsilon^-2) in the practical discussion
No classical runtime comparison on the same task

notes: Paper states the method can be used on digital quantum computers and analog quantum simulators; no specific device is named, so hardware.type is not specified.

No explicit qubit count is given because the method is formulated for an N-qubit many-body system; num_qubits is therefore inferred from the problem size when instantiated, but not explicitly reported as a circuit register size.
The paper explicitly states the algorithm runs in time polynomial in N, inverse variance/width, and inverse error.
The paper proves polynomial scaling for the algorithm, but does not demonstrate a practical quantum advantage over classical methods.
